Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Start
slides.transcript: Welcome to Module 1, Understanding Data in Informatics. This module is the foundation for the rest of IAN 603. Before we clean, transform, query, or model data, we need to understand what the data represents, how it is organized, and whether it is trustworthy enough for the task. We will use small examples and one running patient-encounter dataset so the ideas remain concrete. The goal is not to memorize vocabulary. The goal is to build a habit: understand the data first, then make technical decisions. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a hospital combining patient tables, device JSON, and clinical notes. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: What this module is really about
slides.transcript: This module is really about meaning. Two columns can both be stored as integers and still require completely different analytical treatment. A ZIP code uses digits but is a label. A satisfaction score may use one through five but represents ordered categories. A visit count is a true count. Celsius temperature is a measurement with equal differences but without a meaningful true zero. That is why we do not let the software dtype make the analytical decision for us. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, an e-commerce team preparing customer, purchase, and web-event data. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Learning map
slides.transcript: Here is the workflow we will follow. First, identify how the dataset is organized. Second, assess whether the values are trustworthy enough for the intended use. Third, classify variables by meaning. Fourth, use that meaning to choose summaries, charts, and preprocessing. Finally, implement those choices in Python or PostgreSQL. This order is important. Technical transformations should follow conceptual decisions, not replace them. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a university analyzing student records, surveys, and learning-platform activity. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Running case
slides.transcript: We will reuse these variables throughout the module. Patient ID is an identifier. Triage level is an ordered category. Temperature is a measurement. Emergency visits is a count. Device payload is nested JSON, and a clinical note is free text. Notice that the questions are different. Some questions are about dataset organization. Others are about measurement meaning. Others are about numeric behavior. Learning to identify which question you are answering is one of the most important skills in this module. Connect this idea to a hospital combining patient tables, device JSON, and clinical notes. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Four different questions
slides.transcript: The phrase data type is often used too broadly. In this course, we separate four layers. Data organization describes the form of the dataset. Measurement scale describes the meaning of one variable. Numeric behavior asks whether a quantitative concept comes from counting or measuring. Technical representation describes how software stores the value. A single variable can have an answer at several layers, and those answers are not interchangeable. Connect this idea to an e-commerce team preparing customer, purchase, and web-event data. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Same storage, different meaning
slides.transcript: This table shows why storage alone is not enough. ZIP codes may look numeric, but arithmetic on them is meaningless. Satisfaction ratings use numbers but represent ordered categories. Emergency visits are true counts. Celsius temperature is a numeric measurement, but its zero point is arbitrary. When you see a numeric-looking column, first ask what the numbers mean in the real world. Only after that should you choose summaries, encodings, or models. slides.title: Data organization overview
slides.transcript: The first major question is how the dataset is organized. Structured data follows a predefined schema. Semi-structured data has named fields but allows flexibility and nesting. Unstructured data does not naturally arrive as rows and columns. These categories describe organization. A structured table can still have missing values, duplicate records, or poorly defined variables. Organization and quality are separate issues. Connect this idea to a hospital combining patient tables, device JSON, and clinical notes. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Structured data
slides.transcript: Structured data follows a stable arrangement. Relational databases are a classic example because each row follows a known set of columns and types. CSV and Parquet files can also contain structured data. The benefit is predictability. We can validate and query fields consistently. But structured does not mean correct. A structured table can still contain duplicates, missing values, inconsistent categories, or impossible measurements. A useful project question is: what preparation step is required before analysis can even begin? A relational table may be ready for profiling, JSON may need flattening, and free text may need NLP or another extraction step. The form of the data changes the engineering path, but it does not by itself tell us whether the data is high quality.

slides.title: Structured example
slides.transcript: This structured table is easy to scan because every row follows the same columns. But the columns do not all have the same analytical meaning. Patient ID and ZIP code are labels. Date of birth is temporal. Sex and blood type are categorical. This is a useful example of the distinction between dataset organization and variable meaning. The dataset is structured, but each variable still needs its own classification. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a university analyzing student records, surveys, and learning-platform activity, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Semi-structured data
slides.transcript: Semi-structured data has some organization without requiring every record to look exactly the same. JSON is a common example. Fields have names, but values can be nested, and different records may contain different keys. That flexibility is useful for APIs, devices, logs, and fast-changing applications. The tradeoff is that analysts often need to flatten records, handle optional fields, and manage schema changes before analysis. A useful project question is: what preparation step is required before analysis can even begin? A relational table may be ready for profiling, JSON may need flattening, and free text may need NLP or another extraction step. The form of the data changes the engineering path, but it does not by itself tell us whether the data is high quality.

slides.title: Nested JSON example
slides.transcript: This JSON record is self-describing because the keys tell us what each value represents. But it is not a flat table. Heart rate is nested inside metrics, and latitude and longitude are nested inside location. A second record could add oxygen saturation or omit sleep hours. Before analysis, we often flatten the JSON into columns. But flattening is only a structural step. We still need to understand units, missingness, and the analytical meaning of the extracted fields. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an e-commerce team preparing customer, purchase, and web-event data, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Unstructured data
slides.transcript: Unstructured data does not naturally arrive as a table. A clinical note contains useful information, but the meaning is embedded in text. An image contains visual information. Audio contains signals over time. To analyze these sources, we usually need an extraction step such as NLP, computer vision, OCR, or speech processing. After extraction, some information may become structured features that can be analyzed alongside relational data. A useful project question is: what preparation step is required before analysis can even begin? A relational table may be ready for profiling, JSON may need flattening, and free text may need NLP or another extraction step. The form of the data changes the engineering path, but it does not by itself tell us whether the data is high quality.

slides.title: Compare data forms
slides.transcript: This comparison focuses on the preparation problem. Structured data is already tabular, so we can usually begin with profiling and cleaning. Semi-structured data may need normalization or flattening. Unstructured data usually requires feature extraction or annotation before it can be analyzed using ordinary tabular methods. Real informatics projects often combine all three forms, so understanding the organization tells you what preparation work comes first. slides.title: Volume, velocity, variety
slides.transcript: You may hear modern data described using the three Vs: volume, velocity, and variety. Volume is about scale. Velocity is about how quickly data arrives or must be processed. Variety is about the different forms of data. This module focuses mainly on variety. But in real systems, all three interact. A small JSON file and a streaming feed of millions of JSON events may use the same format but require very different engineering solutions. Connect this idea to an e-commerce team preparing customer, purchase, and web-event data. slides.title: Data quality overview
slides.transcript: Now we move from organization to quality. A dataset can be perfectly structured and still be unsuitable for analysis. Quality is contextual. Data that is acceptable for a monthly report may be too stale for a real-time dashboard. Quality is also evidence-based. An unusual value should be investigated before we automatically delete or replace it. We will use six dimensions and a five-step workflow to reason about quality. In practice, quality rules should be tied to a use case. A fifteen-minute delay may be acceptable for a monthly report but unacceptable for a real-time alert. Likewise, an unusual physiological value should often be flagged and investigated rather than automatically deleted. Good cleaning preserves evidence and documents uncertainty.

slides.title: Six quality dimensions
slides.transcript: These six dimensions give us a practical checklist. Accuracy asks whether a value reflects reality. Completeness asks whether required information is present. Consistency asks whether the same concept is represented compatibly. Timeliness asks whether the data is current enough. Uniqueness asks whether entities appear the intended number of times. Validity checks whether values follow documented rules. The dimensions can overlap, so treat them as a way to organize investigation rather than as perfectly separate boxes. In practice, quality rules should be tied to a use case. A fifteen-minute delay may be acceptable for a monthly report but unacceptable for a real-time alert. Likewise, an unusual physiological value should often be flagged and investigated rather than automatically deleted. Good cleaning preserves evidence and documents uncertainty.

slides.title: Accuracy vs validity
slides.transcript: Validity and accuracy are related but different. Validity asks whether a value fits a documented rule. Accuracy asks whether the value reflects reality. A temperature can fall inside an allowed range and still be inaccurate because of a sensor problem or data-entry error. Validity is often easier to automate. Accuracy may require comparison with the source system, another measurement, or domain knowledge. This distinction prevents us from assuming that passing a validation rule proves the value is true. In practice, quality rules should be tied to a use case. A fifteen-minute delay may be acceptable for a monthly report but unacceptable for a real-time alert. Likewise, an unusual physiological value should often be flagged and investigated rather than automatically deleted. Good cleaning preserves evidence and documents uncertainty.

slides.title: Completeness vs uniqueness
slides.transcript: Completeness and uniqueness are different problems. Completeness asks whether needed values are present. The seriousness depends on the field and the use case. Missing email may be acceptable while missing patient ID may be critical. Uniqueness asks whether one real-world entity appears more than intended. Exact duplicate rows are easy to detect. Duplicate entities under different identifiers are harder and may require entity-resolution methods. Always distinguish missing information from repeated identity. In practice, quality rules should be tied to a use case. A fifteen-minute delay may be acceptable for a monthly report but unacceptable for a real-time alert. Likewise, an unusual physiological value should often be flagged and investigated rather than automatically deleted. Good cleaning preserves evidence and documents uncertainty.

slides.title: Consistency vs timeliness
slides.transcript: Consistency asks whether the same concept is represented the same way. Mixed date formats, category labels, and units can create serious interpretation problems. Timeliness is different. It asks whether the data is current enough for the decision. A fifteen-minute delay may be excellent for a monthly reporting process but unacceptable for an emergency monitoring system. Both dimensions require documentation: shared definitions for consistency and timestamps or refresh expectations for timeliness. In practice, quality rules should be tied to a use case. A fifteen-minute delay may be acceptable for a monthly report but unacceptable for a real-time alert. Likewise, an unusual physiological value should often be flagged and investigated rather than automatically deleted. Good cleaning preserves evidence and documents uncertainty.

slides.title: Quality workflow
slides.transcript: A practical quality workflow has five steps. First, profile the data. Second, detect potential issues. Third, investigate the source and context. Only then decide whether to correct, retain, exclude, impute, or flag the value. Finally, document what happened. This sequence creates an audit trail and reduces the risk of silently changing legitimate unusual values. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an e-commerce team preparing customer, purchase, and web-event data, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Heart-rate quality scenario
slides.transcript: The heart-rate scenario shows why quality work requires judgment. Minus one is clearly incompatible with a normal heart-rate measurement. A blank value is a completeness problem. Two hundred is unusual, but it may be physiologically possible in some circumstances. That means we investigate rather than automatically delete it. Quality rules help us identify records that deserve attention. They do not replace domain reasoning. In practice, quality rules should be tied to a use case. A fifteen-minute delay may be acceptable for a monthly report but unacceptable for a real-time alert. Likewise, an unusual physiological value should often be flagged and investigated rather than automatically deleted. Good cleaning preserves evidence and documents uncertainty.

slides.title: Quality actions
slides.transcript: After identifying a quality problem, we still need a response. Sometimes we can correct a value. Sometimes we retain it. Sometimes we exclude it from one analysis without deleting it from the source. Sometimes we impute missing information. Often, a quality flag is the most transparent choice when uncertainty remains. The objective is not to make the dataset look perfect. It is to make limitations explicit and manageable. In practice, quality rules should be tied to a use case. A fifteen-minute delay may be acceptable for a monthly report but unacceptable for a real-time alert. Likewise, an unusual physiological value should often be flagged and investigated rather than automatically deleted. Good cleaning preserves evidence and documents uncertainty.

slides.title: Measurement scale overview
slides.transcript: Now we move from quality to variable meaning. Measurement scale tells us which comparisons and arithmetic operations are defensible. Nominal and ordinal are categorical scales. Interval and ratio are numeric scales. The key questions are whether order exists, whether differences have a consistent meaning, and whether zero represents the absence of the measured quantity. The easiest way to classify a variable is to ask what statements are meaningful in the real world. Can values only be different, can they be ordered, are differences meaningful, and does zero mean absence? Those questions are more reliable than looking at whether the software stores the column as an integer or floating-point number.

slides.title: Categorical vs numeric
slides.transcript: The broadest split is categorical versus numeric. Categorical variables represent labels or ordered levels. Nominal and ordinal belong here. Numeric variables represent quantities. Interval and ratio belong here. Do not decide by looking only at the characters in the column. A ZIP code contains digits but is categorical. A satisfaction score uses numbers but usually represents ordered categories. Connect this idea to a university analyzing student records, surveys, and learning-platform activity. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Measurement decision tree
slides.transcript: This decision tree provides a simple reasoning process. First, ask whether the values are labels or quantities. If they are labels, ask whether a meaningful order exists. If they are quantities, ask whether the scale has a true zero. This framework works well for many common variables, but domain context still matters. When unsure, explain which comparisons or arithmetic statements would make real-world sense. The easiest way to classify a variable is to ask what statements are meaningful in the real world. Can values only be different, can they be ordered, are differences meaningful, and does zero mean absence? Those questions are more reliable than looking at whether the software stores the column as an integer or floating-point number.

slides.title: Nominal scale
slides.transcript: Nominal variables distinguish categories without placing them in a meaningful order. Blood types are different, but one blood type is not greater than another. ZIP codes and patient IDs are common traps because they may contain digits. Counts and proportions are natural summaries, and bar charts are usually a good starting visualization. The important rule is not to invent numerical meaning for a label. The easiest way to classify a variable is to ask what statements are meaningful in the real world. Can values only be different, can they be ordered, are differences meaningful, and does zero mean absence? Those questions are more reliable than looking at whether the software stores the column as an integer or floating-point number.

slides.title: Nominal visualization
slides.transcript: A bar chart is a natural display for a nominal variable. The bar lengths show counts, which are quantitative. The category labels themselves are not treated as measurements. We can reorder the categories by frequency or by a conventional order without implying that O minus A has any numerical meaning. This is a good example of matching a visualization to the measurement structure. The easiest way to classify a variable is to ask what statements are meaningful in the real world. Can values only be different, can they be ordered, are differences meaningful, and does zero mean absence? Those questions are more reliable than looking at whether the software stores the column as an integer or floating-point number.

slides.title: Ordinal scale
slides.transcript: Ordinal variables have a meaningful order. Emergent is more severe than urgent, and urgent is more severe than non-urgent. But the distance between those levels is not necessarily equal. That means numeric codes can preserve rank while still requiring caution. Medians, percentiles, and ordered displays often respect the structure better than treating the values as ordinary continuous numbers. The easiest way to classify a variable is to ask what statements are meaningful in the real world. Can values only be different, can they be ordered, are differences meaningful, and does zero mean absence? Those questions are more reliable than looking at whether the software stores the column as an integer or floating-point number.

slides.title: Likert caution
slides.transcript: Likert-style responses illustrate ordinal data well. A five is higher than a four, but the psychological distance from one to two may not equal the distance from four to five. Means are commonly reported in practice, particularly for composite scales. But for a single coarse item, medians, distributions, and rank-based summaries may better respect the measurement assumptions. The important point is to recognize the assumption rather than use the mean automatically. Connect this idea to an e-commerce team preparing customer, purchase, and web-event data. A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Interval scale
slides.transcript: Interval scales support meaningful differences. Celsius temperature is the classic example. A difference of five degrees has the same interpretation anywhere on the scale. But zero Celsius is not the absence of temperature. Because the zero point is arbitrary, ratio statements such as twenty degrees being twice ten degrees are not meaningful. The easiest way to classify a variable is to ask what statements are meaningful in the real world. Can values only be different, can they be ordered, are differences meaningful, and does zero mean absence? Those questions are more reliable than looking at whether the software stores the column as an integer or floating-point number.

slides.title: Ratio scale
slides.transcript: Ratio scales have equal differences and a meaningful zero. Zero visits means no visits occurred. Zero elapsed seconds means no time elapsed. Because the zero point represents absence, ratio statements can be meaningful. Four visits can be twice two visits. Ratio variables support a wide range of arithmetic, although distribution, units, and context still affect which summaries are useful. The easiest way to classify a variable is to ask what statements are meaningful in the real world. Can values only be different, can they be ordered, are differences meaningful, and does zero mean absence? Those questions are more reliable than looking at whether the software stores the column as an integer or floating-point number.

slides.title: Interval vs ratio
slides.transcript: Interval and ratio variables can look similar because both are numeric and support meaningful differences. The major distinction is the zero point. Celsius zero is a reference point, not the absence of temperature. Zero visits means no visits occurred. That difference determines whether ratio statements are meaningful. When classifying a numeric variable, ask what zero means in the real-world measurement process. The easiest way to classify a variable is to ask what statements are meaningful in the real world. Can values only be different, can they be ordered, are differences meaningful, and does zero mean absence? Those questions are more reliable than looking at whether the software stores the column as an integer or floating-point number.

slides.title: Discrete vs continuous
slides.transcript: Numeric variables can also be classified by how the values are generated. Discrete variables usually come from counting events or units. Continuous variables come from measurement and conceptually can take values along a range. Do not confuse the stored precision with the concept. A device may report a continuous physiological measurement as a whole number because that is how the instrument records it. The easiest way to classify a variable is to ask what statements are meaningful in the real world. Can values only be different, can they be ordered, are differences meaningful, and does zero mean absence? Those questions are more reliable than looking at whether the software stores the column as an integer or floating-point number.

slides.title: When integer storage misleads
slides.transcript: This slide shows four columns that could all be stored as integers. Heart rate is a measurement recorded to whole units. Emergency visits is a count. Patient ID is a label. Satisfaction is ordinal. The same technical dtype supports four different analytical meanings. This is why the correct question is not, what dtype does pandas show? The correct question is, how was this value generated and what comparisons make sense? Connect this idea to a hospital combining patient tables, device JSON, and clinical notes. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Common classification traps
slides.transcript: These are common classification traps. The visual appearance of a value can tempt us to classify too quickly. ZIP codes and patient IDs are labels. Satisfaction is ordered but not necessarily equally spaced. Heart rate may be stored as an integer while representing a measurement. ER visits is a count. Celsius temperature is interval rather than ratio. When in doubt, describe the variable in a sentence and ask what operations make real-world sense. slides.title: From type to decision
slides.transcript: Classification should lead to an analytical decision. Once you understand the variable, choose summaries that respect the scale, visualizations that show the intended comparison, and encodings that do not introduce false structure. Then validate the transformed result. This is not a rigid cookbook. Distribution, study design, and analytical goals still matter, but measurement meaning gives us a defensible starting point. Connect this idea to a university analyzing student records, surveys, and learning-platform activity. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Summary choices
slides.transcript: Choosing a summary is a conceptual decision. Counts and proportions fit nominal categories naturally. Ordinal variables often support medians and percentiles. Numeric variables may use means and standard deviations when the mean is meaningful and the distribution is appropriate. Skewed numeric data often benefits from median and interquartile range. Do not apply the same summary mechanically to every column in a dataframe. Connect this idea to a hospital combining patient tables, device JSON, and clinical notes. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Visualization choices
slides.transcript: Visualization should respect the variable structure. Bar charts work well for nominal categories. Ordered bars preserve the order of ordinal categories. Histograms show the distribution of continuous numeric variables. Scatterplots show relationships between two numeric variables. A chart should make the intended comparison easier without adding structure that the data does not contain. For example, connecting unordered categories with a line can accidentally imply continuity. Connect this idea to an e-commerce team preparing customer, purchase, and web-event data. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Encoding choices overview
slides.transcript: Encoding changes how software represents a variable. It does not change the underlying meaning. Nominal variables often use one-hot indicators. Ordinal variables may use ordered categorical dtypes or explicit ordinal codes. Numeric variables can remain numeric and may be scaled for methods that need comparable feature scales. Counts should remain conceptually counts even if a model later transforms them. The representation should support, not redefine, the concept. Preprocessing is not neutral: it tells software how to interpret the variable. One-hot encoding avoids inventing rank for nominal categories; ordinal coding preserves a known order; scaling changes numerical representation but not conceptual meaning. In predictive work, learned preprocessing should be fitted only on training data so evaluation remains honest.

slides.title: Membership tier example
slides.transcript: Membership tier is an ordered category, but it can be represented in more than one way. An ordinal code preserves the rank from Bronze through Platinum. A one-hot representation avoids expressing the category as a single numeric distance. Neither changes the underlying business meaning. The better representation depends on how the analytical method will interpret the values. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a hospital combining patient tables, device JSON, and clinical notes, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: One-hot encoding
slides.transcript: One-hot encoding creates separate indicator columns. With Bronze as the reference category, the generated columns represent Silver, Gold, and Platinum. Bronze is represented by all zeros. This is useful when we do not want a model to treat categories as points on one numeric line. The tradeoff is dimensionality. Variables with many categories can create many columns. Preprocessing is not neutral: it tells software how to interpret the variable. One-hot encoding avoids inventing rank for nominal categories; ordinal coding preserves a known order; scaling changes numerical representation but not conceptual meaning. In predictive work, learned preprocessing should be fitted only on training data so evaluation remains honest.

slides.title: Ordinal encoding
slides.transcript: Ordinal encoding maps ordered categories to ordered numbers. The representation is compact and preserves rank. But some analytical methods may interpret the gaps between codes as equal. That is an additional assumption, not something guaranteed by the original category labels. Whenever you use ordinal codes, document the intended order and understand how the downstream model uses numeric distance. The easiest way to classify a variable is to ask what statements are meaningful in the real world. Can values only be different, can they be ordered, are differences meaningful, and does zero mean absence? Those questions are more reliable than looking at whether the software stores the column as an integer or floating-point number.

slides.title: Data leakage
slides.transcript: One important preprocessing idea is data leakage. If we fit a scaler or learned encoder using the entire dataset before evaluation, information from validation or test data can influence the transformation. A safer workflow fits learned preprocessing on the training data and applies the fitted transformation to validation or test data. Module 1 is not a machine-learning module, but this habit is worth establishing now because preprocessing can affect the honesty of later evaluation. Preprocessing is not neutral: it tells software how to interpret the variable. One-hot encoding avoids inventing rank for nominal categories; ordinal coding preserves a known order; scaling changes numerical representation but not conceptual meaning. In predictive work, learned preprocessing should be fitted only on training data so evaluation remains honest.

slides.title: Python lab roadmap
slides.transcript: Now we move into the guided Python lab. The code is intentionally short. We will create a small dataframe, inspect it, assign meaningful dtypes, encode categories, scale selected numeric features, flatten JSON, and add basic quality checks. The most important rule is simple: inspect and understand first, transform second. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. slides.title: Assign meaningful pandas dtypes
slides.transcript: Now we align the pandas dtypes more closely with the concepts. Sex becomes a categorical variable. Triage level and membership tier use ordered categorical dtypes with the intended order written explicitly. Patient ID becomes a string because it identifies a record rather than measuring an amount. The dtype is now more informative, but it still does not replace documentation about the meaning of each variable. Preprocessing is not neutral: it tells software how to interpret the variable. slides.title: One-hot encode a nominal variable
slides.transcript: This code one-hot encodes the nominal variable sex. The goal is to represent categories without assigning them a single numerical rank. With drop first, one category becomes the reference. Handle unknown provides a defined behavior if a later dataset contains a category not seen during fitting. The key idea is that the encoding follows from the nominal meaning of the variable. The easiest way to classify a variable is to ask what statements are meaningful in the real world. Can values only be different, can they be ordered, are differences meaningful, and does zero mean absence? Those questions are more reliable than looking at whether the software stores the column as an integer or floating-point number.

slides.title: Ordinal encode an ordered variable

That matters because software should not guess the intended order from alphabetical sorting. The resulting codes are compact and ordered. But remember the earlier caution: some models may treat the numeric gaps as equal, so the representation must fit the method and interpretation. slides.title: Flatten semi-structured JSON
slides.transcript: Pandas json normalize can flatten nested JSON into columns. Nested keys such as metrics heart rate and metrics steps become analytical fields. Notice what happens when a key exists in only one record. The other record receives a missing value. Flattening solves the structural problem, but it creates new quality questions about missingness, units, and field meaning. Technical normalization is only the beginning of analytical understanding. A useful project question is: what preparation step is required before analysis can even begin? A relational table may be ready for profiling, JSON may need flattening, and free text may need NLP or another extraction step. The form of the data changes the engineering path, but it does not by itself tell us whether the data is high quality.

slides.title: Add basic quality checks
slides.transcript: The final Python step translates some quality rules into code. We inspect missingness, verify identifier uniqueness, test simple validity rules, and review category frequencies. Assertions are useful for teaching because they make a rule explicit. Production pipelines usually need richer logging and exception handling, but the principle is the same. Quality rules should be documented and checked consistently. In practice, quality rules should be tied to a use case. A fifteen-minute delay may be acceptable for a monthly report but unacceptable for a real-time alert. Likewise, an unusual physiological value should often be flagged and investigated rather than automatically deleted. Good cleaning preserves evidence and documents uncertainty.

slides.title: Five key takeaways
slides.transcript: Let's reduce the module to five ideas. First, separate dataset organization from variable meaning and technical storage. Second, assess quality before trusting the analysis. Third, use measurement scale to decide which comparisons and summaries make sense. Fourth, remember that a dtype does not define analytical meaning. Fifth, make preprocessing choices deliberately and document why they are appropriate. Do not treat this as a list to memorize.
